power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

# display table -----------------------------------

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.137", "p ≥ 0.05"), Sentence = c("MCMC chain convergence for the baseline intercept was formally confirmed using Geweke's diagnostic (Z = -1.49, p = 0.137), indicating that the post-burn-in iterations reached stationary equilibrium.", "The remaining 14 evaluated candidate clusters did not reach statistical significance (p ≥ 0.05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Although preventable, maternal mortality remains a global challenge.
Its burden is disproportionately concentrated in low-and middle-income settings.
Substantial subnational geographical variations also persist within countries, driven by underlying socioeconomic disparities and unequal access to quality healthcare services.

Here we propose a spatial consensus framework combining frequentist and Bayesian models to overcome variance instability in small-area estimates, mapping maternal mortality risk among Black women in Brazil to guide equitable public health interventions.
Using nationwide surveillance data (2019-2024), we applied a spatial Poisson probability model to detect high-rate clusters of maternal mortality among Black women.
Concurrently, Bayesian hierarchical spatial models were fitted to smooth small-area rates and stabilize variance.
Results from both approaches were integrated into a five-level risk typology to categorize Brazilian municipalities.
National aggregate reductions in Brazilian maternal mortality mask profound, spatially concentrated racial inequities.

The spatial classification of risk scenarios identified 13 municipalities with Confirmed Critical Risk, 28 municipalities with Persistent Regional Risk, 12 municipalities with a Local Excess Alert, and 4 exhibiting Epidemiological Silence.
The vast majority remained at the Expected Risk Level.
The proposed spatial consensus framework translates complex spatio-temporal modeling into an operational typology for surveillance systems.

This approach bridges the gap between spatial analytics and public health decision-making, providing a replicable tool to address structural racial disparities in maternal health within decentralized health systems.

text.text: Consequently, achieving health equity extends beyond considerations of optional normative objective, but a practical prerequisite for improving health outcomes, health system efficiency and for national progress.
Routine public health surveillance typically relies on conventional frequentist indicators, such as raw Standardized Mortality Ratios (SMRs).
However, in nationwide contexts like Brazil, severe demographic heterogeneity introduces extreme variance instability.
Municipal volumes of live births range from single digits to hundreds of thousands, generating a Coefficient of Variation well above 500% around a heavily right-skewed distribution.
Under such population asymmetry, a single maternal death in a small municipality can spuriously inflate raw rates, introducing substantial spatial noise into geographic prioritization.

To mitigate this instability, Bayesian spatial smoothing techniques, such as Conditional Autoregressive (CAR) models, are widely employed to 'borrow strength' across neighboring jurisdictions, effectively stabilizing variance while capturing broad spatial trends. 10, 11 Despite its advantages, Bayesian spatial smoothing exhibits inherent methodological limitations.

text.text: We used publicly available data of maternal deaths and live births by municipality occurred from 2019 to 2024.
Maternal death data were retrieved from the SIM/DATASUS official maternal mortality dataset (DOMAT), which includes deaths after investigation by local Maternal Death Surveillance Committees.

The utilization of this consolidated system is supported by national methodological benchmarks for maternal mortality monitoring in Brazil. 18 Information on recorded race/color was obtained from the Mortality Information System (SIM) database, which categorizes this field into five official groups: White (branca), Black (preta), Asian (amarela), Mixed-race (parda), and Indigenous (indígena).

Maternal mortality in Brazil is still far from the target established by PAHO/WHO of fewer than 30 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030.
Even in the end of the analysed period, the MMRs in 2024 reached 44.2 and 47.2 for White and combined Black women, respectively.
Counterfactual sensitivity analysis confirmed that the observed surge in the MMR among White women during the 2021 pandemic peak was substantially driven by a denominator artifact.
Between 2019 and 2021, live births contracted by 9.90% among White women-a reduction 2.5 times sharper than that observed among combined Black women (-3.91%).
This differential birth decline artificially added 10.32 deaths per 100,000 live births to the observed MMR of White women, compared to an effect of 3.56 points among combined Black women.

When holding the live birth denominator constant at 2019 pre-pandemic levels, the counterfactual 2021 MMR for White women dropped from 104.3 to 94 per 100,000 live births, suggesting that differential denominator contraction contributed to the apparent racial inversion.

Furthermore, while registered maternal deaths rose in both groups, the lower relative increase observed among combined Black women (+94•3% vs. +152•9% in White women) is consistent with potential ascertainment bias and differential underreporting during public health system collapse, as widely documented in the Brazilian context. 26, 27 Beyond spatial concentration, the stark divergence in the underlying causes of maternal death between racial groups exposes deep-seated inequities in the quality of clinical care.

This excess of direct obstetric mortality among combined Black women reflects systemic barriers in the continuum of care, including lower quality of prenatal coverage, delayed referral for high-risk pregnancies, and the structural phenomenon of obstetric 'pilgrimage', wherein marginalized women are forced to seek care across multiple hospital facilities during labor. 6, 28 Addressing racial disparities in Brazilian maternal mortality therefore requires not only geographic targeting, but also institutional reforms to eliminate racial bias in clinical decision-making and ensure equitable access to tertiary obstetric critical care. 29 The substantial reduction in range from raw SMR to Bayesian spatial RR highlights the importance of spatial smoothing when analyzing rare health events in small populations.

The integration of Bayesian spatial smoothing and flexible spatial scan statistics (FleXScan) into a unified classification matrix can, potentially, provide indications towards a robust decision-making framework for epidemiological surveillance and public health action.

By cross-referencing model-based posterior probabilities with nonparametric cluster detection, municipalities were categorized into five operational risk scenarios, each reflecting distinct spatial dynamics, surveillance implications, and targeted intervention strategies.
This approach allows a more direct basis to formulate context-based health action and/or policies within Brazilian healthcare system -SUS.

text.text: Methodologically, this consensus framework bridges the gap between discrete cluster detection and continuous risk smoothing, filtering out variance instability while unmasking spatial vulnerabilities that a single method would miss.
Operationally, it provides public health decisionmakers with a two-tiered strategy: immediate, targeted interventions and long-term structural planning.
This study has limitations inherent to spatial epidemiological designs utilizing secondary administrative data.

First, despite using the consolidated DOMAT database and incorporating post-investigation reclassifications by Maternal Death Surveillance Committees, residual under-reporting and misclassification of maternal status on Death Certificates remain plausible, particularly in remote or under-resourced municipalities.
Nevertheless, our framework explicitly addresses this constraint by establishing the 'Epidemiological Silence' scenario to systematically flag suspected under-reporting.

This methodological discrepancy between birth and death registration systems may introduce racial misclassification bias or lead to missing data in secondary records.This study demonstrates that national aggregate reductions in Brazilian maternal mortality mask profound, spatially concentrated racial inequities.
Combined Black women consistently experienced higher MMRs than White women across the pre-and post-pandemic periods.
Counterfactual analysis proved that the temporary 2021 spike observed among White women was an artifact of differential birth contraction rather than a true shift in racial vulnerability.
Achieving the Sustainable Development Goal target by 2030 remains unfeasible for Brazil without directly eliminating excess mortality among combined Black women.

Public health authorities must leverage spatial consensus scenarios to prioritize emergency resource deployment, strengthen local Maternal Death Surveillance Committees, and enforce anti-racist, equitable clinical protocols across maternal healthcare networks.
